beats.text: You’ve been told gift cards expire, but Starbucks’ cards never do.

In the United States the coffee chain’s stored‑value cards carry no expiration date and no service fees. Instead, Starbucks estimates the portion that will never be redeemed and records that breakage as revenue over time. The estimate follows historical redemption patterns for each market and includes any required remittance to state unclaimed‑property agencies.

A 2024 Bankrate survey of 2,373 U.S. adults found 43 % hold at least one unused gift card, voucher or store credit. Respondents reported a combined $27 billion in unused balances, averaging $244 per holder and a median of $100. Those figures represent an estimate based on an online YouGov sample collected in August 2024.

Federal unclaimed‑property laws require retailers to remit a share of dormant balances to state authorities after a dormancy period. Starbucks’ breakage accounting incorporates that remittance, so the revenue it books is net of any state claim. The same rules apply to other U.S. retailers, limiting how quickly they can move unspent value onto their books.

Retailers must show gift‑card balances on their balance sheets. Starbucks reported $1.751 billion in stored‑value and loyalty balances at the end of fiscal 2025, up from $1.718 billion a year earlier.

At the same time, Starbucks booked $200.4 million of breakage revenue from company‑operated stores and $22.0 million from licensed stores in fiscal 2025. Those figures follow the company’s estimate of how much loaded value will never be redeemed.

The company arrives at those numbers by comparing the $15.245 billion loaded during the year with the $15.199 billion recognized from redemptions and breakage, then applying its internal model. The model also accounts for state unclaimed‑property remittances, so the recorded breakage is net of any claim.

To turn those balances into revenue, Starbucks uses an accounting estimate called breakage. It projects the fraction of loaded value that will remain dormant after the statutory dormancy period, subtracts any amount the state is likely to claim, and records the remainder gradually as income. That estimate becomes part of the company’s reported earnings each quarter.

Starbucks’ stored‑value cards never expire and carry no service fees. The company looks at past redemption patterns for each market, then estimates the fraction that will never used. That estimate also subtracts what state unclaimed‑property laws are likely to claim, so the breakage figure is net of any government take. Federal unclaimed‑property statutes require retailers to hold the balance for at least five years before it can be deemed abandoned.

In fiscal 2025 Starbucks recorded $200.4 million of breakage from company‑operated stores and $22.0 million from licensed stores. The prior year showed $187.6 million and $20.0 million, and 2023 reported $196.1 million and $18.9 million respectively. Starbucks spreads the breakage amount into quarterly earnings, recognizing it gradually as cards are redeemed.

Adding the two lines gives us $222.4 million of breakage revenue for fiscal 2025, $207.6 million for 2024, and $215.0 million for 2023. That calculation is ours, not the company’s. Because breakage is an accounting estimate, the actual amount of unused balances could differ.

Darden records gift‑card sales only when the cards are redeemed. Its cards carry no expiration dates or dormancy fees. The company estimates breakage over an expected redemption period of twelve years and revises those estimates as redemptions occur.
In fiscal 2026 Darden loaded $760.2 million onto new cards, logged $751.9 million as redemptions and breakage, and its deferred gift‑card liability rose from $628.8 million to $636.7 million.
Our arithmetic shows the unspent pool grew by $7.9 million over the year.
Darden notes that unclaimed‑property laws are highly complex and force the company to make many subjective assumptions, estimates and judgments.
A half‑percentage swing in Darden’s breakage estimate would shift reported breakage income by $3.6 million for fiscal 2026, according to its filing.

Darden records gift‑card revenue only when cards are redeemed. It assumes most cards are used within a twelve‑year window, but it updates that window and the breakage rate as actual redemptions come in, acknowledging the figures are estimates, not guarantees.

If the company’s breakage rate is off by just 0.5 percentage points, the $3.6 million swing represents less than one percent of Darden’s total annual revenue, yet it still moves money from a future liability into current profit, changing the balance sheet and tax picture.

The filing warns that actual breakage could be higher or lower than the recorded amount, because consumer behavior, economic shifts, or legal changes can alter redemption patterns over the twelve‑year horizon.

Because the breakage figure is an estimate, any excess unredeemed balance that later becomes subject to unclaimed‑property law may have to be turned over to the state, reducing the net profit the company finally keeps.

Federal law says a store gift card can only expire if the balance stays valid for at least five years after it is issued or last loaded. A dormancy or service fee may appear only after a full year of inactivity, and no more than one fee per calendar month. Those rules keep retailers from instantly converting every unused cent into revenue.

When a balance remains unclaimed beyond the period allowed by state unclaimed‑property statutes, the retailer must surrender that money to the state. Darden notes that the accounting for those laws is highly complex, relying on subjective assumptions and periodic estimates. If the company’s breakage estimate falls short, the excess ends up in a state treasury rather than the retailer’s bottom line.

Starbucks recorded $222.4 million of breakage revenue in fiscal 2025, its own estimate of unspent balances. That figure represents the portion of Starbucks’ gift‑card balances that the company expects will never be redeemed, and it is booked as revenue over time.

Darden’s accounting shows its unspent pool grew by $7.9 million in fiscal 2026, the amount it expects to keep as breakage. The increase reflects Darden’s estimate of cards that will stay idle after all redemptions are accounted for, and it will be recognized as breakage revenue.

A Bankrate‑YouGov survey of 2,373 U.S. adults, conducted online in August 2024, estimated that households hold about $27 billion in unused gift‑card value. The sample included 1,010 respondents who reported unused balances, and the total is an extrapolation from that group.

Federal rules require a card’s balance to remain valid for at least five years, and state unclaimed‑property statutes can divert any balance that stays idle beyond that period to the state treasury. Because the balance must stay valid for at least five years, any amount that remains untouched after that period may be turned over to the state, reducing the retailer’s ultimate take.

Federal law caps how a retailer can erode a card’s balance. A gift card may only carry an expiration date if the funds stay usable for at least five years after issuance or the last load. A dormancy or inactivity fee can appear only after a full year of no activity, and no more than one fee per calendar month.

Darden’s own filing admits that unclaimed‑property statutes sit among a maze of accounting and legal rules. The company describes the breakage estimate as built on many subjective assumptions, judgments and periodic updates. In other words, the figure it records is a best‑guess, not a precise count of forgotten cards.

Because the five‑year validity floor and the subjective breakage model both shape the numbers, any arithmetic we perform rests on those premises. Our division of the survey total by the number of cards is ours, not the companies’, and it inherits the same uncertainties built into the regulations and the estimates. Thus the final pocket‑share we report should be read as an informed approximation, not an exact ledger.
Our arithmetic shows Starbucks recorded $222.4 million of breakage revenue in fiscal 2025, $207.6 million in 2024 and $215.0 million in 2023.
Darden’s filing shows $760.2 million of new card loads and $751.9 million redeemed, leaving an unspent pool that grew by $7.9 million over the year.

A Bankrate‑YouGov survey of 2,373 U.S. adults estimates $27 billion sits idle on gift cards, meaning roughly 43 percent of adults hold at least one unused card. That means retailers keep the bulk of the unspent value as breakage, the state can claim a share under unclaimed‑property laws, and only a small remainder stays with the cardholder.
